lines.text: A vineyard is a plantation of grapevines cultivated for winemaking, and the English wine industry has experienced a remarkable renaissance over the past two decades. The chalky soils of southern England — particularly in Kent, Sussex, Surrey, and Hampshire — share geological similarities with the Champagne region of France, making them ideal for sparkling wine production. Vines are planted in neat rows along south-facing slopes to maximise sun exposure and drainage. The annual cycle begins with pruning in winter, when dormant vines are cut back to control growth. Spring brings bud break — the first green shoots emerging after months of bare wood. Throughout summer, vineyard workers manage the canopy, thinning leaves to allow sunlight to reach the developing grape clusters. Flowering occurs in early summer; each tiny flower, if successfully pollinated, becomes a grape. The growing season is a constant battle against frost, disease, and unpredictable British weather. Harvest — known as 'vintage' — typically takes place in October, when sugar levels in the grapes reach the ideal balance with acidity. Grapes are picked by hand or by machine, then transported immediately to the winery for pressing. English sparkling wines have won international blind tastings against established Champagne houses, proving that terroir — the unique combination of soil, climate, and geography — matters more than latitude.

lines.text: The dominant English grape varieties are Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, and Pinot Meunier — the same trio used in Champagne.
